text: Pyotr Leonidovich Kapitsa, also known as Peter Kapitza FRS (Russian: Пётр Леонидович Капица, Romanian: Petre Capița; 9 July [O.S. 26 June] 1894 – 8 April 1984), was a leading Soviet Russian physicist and Nobel laureate whose research focused on low-temperature physics. Born in Kronstadt, Russian Empire, to Leonid Petrovich Kapitsa, a military engineer who built fortifications, and Olga Ieronimovna Kapitsa, from a noble Polish Stebnicki family, Kapitsa's family also spoke Romanian besides Russian. His studies were interrupted by the First World War, during which he served as an ambulance driver on the Polish front for two years. He graduated from the Petrograd Polytechnical Institute in 1918; his wife and two children died in the 1918–19 flu epidemic. He subsequently studied in Britain, working for over ten years with Ernest Rutherford at the Cavendish Laboratory at the University of Cambridge, where he founded the influential Kapitza club and served as the first director of the Mond Laboratory from 1930 to 1934. In the 1920s, he developed techniques for creating ultrastrong magnetic fields using high-current pulses in specially constructed air-core electromagnets and discovered in 1928 a linear relationship between resistivity and magnetic field strength in various metals under very strong magnetic fields. In 1934, after returning to Russia to visit his parents, the Soviet Union prevented him from returning to Great Britain. Although his high-magnetic field equipment remained in Cambridge (later facilitated by Rutherford's negotiations with the British government for shipment to the USSR), he shifted his research to low-temperature phenomena, beginning with a critical analysis of existing low-temperature methods. In 1934, he developed new apparatus based on the adiabatic principle for producing significant quantities of liquid helium. He participated in forming the Institute for Physical Problems, using equipment purchased from the Mond Laboratory with Rutherford's assistance after it was clear Kapitsa would not return. In Russia, Kapitsa conducted experiments on liquid helium, culminating in the 1937 discovery of superfluidity, a state of matter linked to superconductivity. He documented the properties of helium-4 superfluid in a series of papers beginning with a letter to the editor of Science on 8 January 1938, reporting the absence of measurable viscosity in liquid helium-4 cooled below 1.8 K, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1978 "for his basic inventions and discoveries in the area of low-temperature physics." In 1939, he developed a new method for air liquefaction using a low-pressure cycle and a special high-efficiency expansion turbine. During World War II, he headed the Department of Oxygen Industry under the USSR Council of Ministers, applying his low-pressure expansion techniques industrially. He invented high-power microwave generators between 1950 and 1955 and discovered a new type of continuous high-pressure plasma discharge with electron temperatures exceeding 1,000,000 K. In November 1945, he quarreled with Lavrentiy Beria, head of the NKVD and in charge of the Soviet atomic bomb project, writing to Joseph Stalin about Beria's lack of physics knowledge and arrogance; Stalin supported Kapitsa, instructing Beria to cooperate with scientists, and Kapitsa refused to meet Beria, stating, "If you want to speak to me, then come to the Institute," though Stalin never met with him. Immediately after the war, prominent Soviet scientists, including Kapitsa, lobbied the government to establish the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology, where Kapitsa taught for many years. From 1957, he was a member of the presidium of the Soviet Academy of Sciences and at his death in 1984 remained the only presidium member not also a member of the Communist Party. In 1966, he was allowed to visit Cambridge to receive the Rutherford Medal and Prize; while dining at his old college, Trinity, he found he did not have the required gown and asked to borrow one, but a servant, upon learning he had last dined at high table thirty-two years prior, returned with his own gown. In 1978, Kapitsa won the Nobel Prize in Physics "for his basic inventions and discoveries in the area of low-temperature physics," sharing it with Arno Allan Penzias and Robert Woodrow Wilson, who won for discovering the cosmic microwave background. Kapitsa resistance is the thermal resistance at the interface between liquid helium and a solid, the Kapitsa–Dirac effect is a quantum mechanical phenomenon involving electron diffraction by a standing wave of light, and the Kapitza number is a dimensionless parameter characterizing the flow of thin fluid films down an incline. Kapitsa had the nickname "Centaurus," originating when his student Shalnikov, asked if his supervisor was human or a beast, replied that he was a Centaurus—capable of being human but also capable of anger and striking with hooves like a horse. He was married in 1927 to Anna Alekseyevna Krylova (1903–1996), daughter of applied mathematician Aleksey Krylov; they had two sons, Sergey (1928–2012), a physicist and demographer, and Andrey (1931–2011), a geographer credited with the discovery and naming of Lake Vostok, the largest subglacial lake in Antarctica, located 4,000 meters below the ice cap. Kapitsa had influence with high-level Soviet officials due to the industrial applications of his discoveries and regularly wrote on science policy, saving both Vladimir Fock and Lev Landau from Stalin's purges in the 1930s by informing Vyacheslav Molotov that Landau was the only one who could solve a critical physics problem. He died on 8 April 1984 in Moscow at the age of 89. A minor planet, 3437 Kapitsa, discovered by Lyudmila Karachkina in 1982, is named after him. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) in 1929 and a Member of the German Academy of Sciences Leopoldina in 1958.
